name: Tilaka

card.summary: A Hindu forehead mark made from ash, sandalwood, clay or kumkum that is worn for devotion and also serves as a distinctive adornment.
card.note: Primarily a religious practice; some traditional cosmetic powders have been associated with lead exposure in research.

quick.overview:
Tilaka (also tilak or tika) is a mark worn mainly on the forehead in Hinduism, made from materials such as sandalwood paste, kumkum (vermilion), sacred ash, clay or turmeric. It signals devotion and sectarian identity, and it is also a visible adornment.

Styles vary by tradition: Vaishnavas wear vertical U-shaped marks, Shaivites three horizontal bands, and Shaktas a red dot. Wikipedia notes it may be applied for decorative purposes as well as religious ones, and it is worn daily or for rites and festivals.
quick.how: The mark is applied by hand or with a small tool as part of worship or on occasions, using the material and pattern of the wearer's tradition. It is also used to welcome guests.
quick.risks: The practice itself is low-risk, but a study of South Asian women in Leeds found traditional cosmetics among practices associated with higher blood lead in pregnancy, so material safety matters.

lead: Tilaka, also spelled tilak or tika, is a mark worn in Hinduism, most often on the forehead at the ajna chakra, or third eye, though it can appear on the neck, hand, chest or arm. Materials include sandalwood paste, kumkum, sacred ash, turmeric and clay.[1][2]
It is primarily a religious sign of devotion and affiliation, but it is also an adornment that changes the look of the face, and in looksmaxxing style discussion it appears as a cultural marking.[2]
Its form varies by denomination: the Vaishnava urdhva pundra uses vertical lines with a U-shape, the Shaiva tripundra uses three horizontal bands, and Shaktas wear a red dot.[1][2]

chain: Apply a tilaka in the tradition's material and pattern
Expresses identity and adorns the face
angle.text: Wearers apply the mark first as an act of devotion; it also acts as a visible facial adornment tied to cultural identity and dress.

paras: Wikipedia describes tilaka as worn daily or for rites of passage and occasions, and used to welcome a guest. Vaishnava marks may be made with gopi-chandan clay; Shaivite tripundra traditionally uses vibhuti, sacred ash.[1][2] Jains use it to mark images of Jinas.[2]

Grokipedia traces the word to Sanskrit tilaka, linked to tila, sesame seed, and describes forehead marks in epic literature such as the Mahabharata and in medieval temple iconography.[1] Hindu scriptures explain the marks' meanings, for example the Shaiva mark as linked to Shiva's powers of will, knowledge and action.[2]
Wikipedia notes tilaka may be applied for decorative purposes, and that the related bindi is now made in many colours and shapes to match clothing.[2]
A study of pregnant South Asian women in Leeds found higher blood lead than among Caucasian women and noted traditional cosmetics among culturally embedded practices that may raise exposure.[3]
No studies found on tilaka for appearance. A Leeds study examined lead exposure linked to cultural practices including traditional cosmetics.[3]
